evals.name: sparse-hardware-kickoff
evals.prompt: my workstation has started freezing hard a few times a week — screen locks up, no mouse, audio loops, have to hold the power button. started maybe two weeks ago? i've already reseated the ram and it still happened twice since. help me figure out what it is. it's a ryzen 5950x box, fedora 42, nvidia 3080, corsair rm850 psu, about 3 years old. i use it for gaming and some llm stuff
evals.expected_output: A structured diagnostic kickoff: separates/states the deviation, starts a comparative specification (what/where/when/extent, IS vs IS-NOT), asks a focused batch of questions (not a 20-question dump), records the RAM reseat as evidence, proposes cheap discriminating tests (journal after freeze, temps, workload correlation) with what each would rule out, and does NOT propose fixes (reinstall/replace PSU) before any cause survives testing.
assertions: Builds a comparative specification covering all four dimensions (what / where / when / extent) with explicit IS and IS-NOT (or 'unknown — to check') entries
Requests missing facts as a focused batch (roughly 8 questions or fewer) with a stated reason for what each answer would discriminate — not an exhaustive question dump
Records the RAM reseat and its failure to help as elimination evidence (referenced in the analysis, not ignored)
Proposes at least two cheap discriminating next steps (e.g. persistent journal after a freeze, temperature/workload correlation, memtest) and names what each result would rule in or out
Proposes no remediation (OS reinstall, PSU/GPU replacement, part purchases) before any cause has been tested — diagnostic actions only
Enumerates 3 or more candidate causes stated as mechanisms (how the cause produces exactly this freeze pattern), not a single committed favorite
States no fabricated facts — no invented log contents, temperatures, or test results presented as observed

evals.name: red-herring-cluster
evals.prompt: Our RKE2 cluster has 6 workers (w1-w6). Since July 22 around 14:00, pods scheduled on w4, w5 and w6 intermittently fail to pull images from our internal registry — timeouts mid-layer, 'context deadline exceeded', maybe 1 in 3 pulls fails. w1-w3 never fail. All six nodes were upgraded to RKE2 1.32.5 on July 21 evening — my colleague is sure the upgrade broke containerd and wants to roll back tonight. More facts: small images (<10MB) almost always pull fine even on w4-w6, big layers fail most often. w4-w6 sit in rack B on switch-B (new switch installed July 22 morning during a network refresh), w1-w3 in rack A on switch-A. The registry VM is in rack A. Pulls from Docker Hub through our proxy also fail on w4-w6, again mostly big layers. Plain ping from every node to the registry is fine. What's going on — should we roll back RKE2 tonight?
evals.expected_output: Rejects the rollback: the upgrade hypothesis fails against the IS-NOT evidence (all 6 nodes upgraded but only 3 affected; onset ~18h after upgrade but same-day as switch-B install; failure follows rack/switch topology and packet size, not container runtime). Identifies a switch-B-class network cause (MTU mismatch / large-frame loss consistent with big-layers-fail-small-succeed-ping-fine) as most probable, and proposes cheap discriminating verification (e.g. large-packet ping with DF bit / iperf through switch-B / check switch MTU config) before any rollback.
assertions: Recommends against rolling back RKE2 tonight, or makes rollback strictly contingent on a discriminating test first

Explicitly refutes the upgrade hypothesis using the given evidence: all six nodes were upgraded but only three are affected, and/or onset (~18h after the upgrade) aligns with the switch-B install instead

Identifies a rack-B / switch-B network path cause of the MTU-mismatch / large-frame-loss class as most probable, consistent with the size signature (big layers fail, small pulls and plain pings succeed)
Proposes a cheap discriminating verification before any action: large-packet ping with DF bit / packet-size sweep, iperf across switch-B, or checking the new switch's MTU/port config
Organizes the evidence as an explicit affected-vs-unaffected comparison (nodes, image sizes, timing, registry source) that a reader can verify at a glance
For at least one proposed test, states what each possible outcome would imply for the competing hypotheses (which candidate dies on which result)

evals.name: day-one-twin-server
evals.prompt: we commissioned a second 'identical' epyc server (srv-b) three weeks ago as a twin to srv-a for our postgres analytics load. srv-b has been ~35% slower on the same queries since day one — it was never fast. same chassis model, same cpu sku, same amount of ram (512GB), same nvme model, same ubuntu 24.04 image via the same ansible playbooks, same postgres version and config. we've already: re-run the playbooks (no config drift found), updated bios to the same version as srv-a, swapped the nvme with a spare (no change). team's current theory is 'bad cpu, RMA it'. before we file the RMA — can you help us troubleshoot this properly?
evals.expected_output: Recognizes a never-worked-right (Day One) deviation: stops hunting for 'what changed' and drives a systematic distinctions hunt against the working twin instead. Treats 'bad cpu' as a weak candidate (no mechanism; uniform 35% deficit atypical for silicon defects). Records the failed swap/playbook/BIOS attempts as elimination evidence. Proposes cheap side-by-side comparisons before RMA: DIMM population/channel config (dmidecode), memory bandwidth (STREAM/mlc), BIOS settings beyond version (NUMA, power/perf profile, cTDP), CPU frequency behavior under load, PCIe link width — each tied to what it would rule in/out.
assertions: Recognizes this as a never-worked-right (Day One) deviation and explicitly redirects the investigation from 'what changed' to 'what differs between srv-b and srv-a'
Treats 'bad CPU, RMA it' as a weak hypothesis with a stated reason (no mechanism offered; a uniform ~35% deficit is atypical of defective silicon) and does not endorse filing the RMA yet
Proposes side-by-side comparison of physical memory configuration — DIMM population / active channels (dmidecode or equivalent) — as a candidate class

Proposes at least three concrete cheap comparisons before RMA (e.g. memory bandwidth benchmark, BIOS settings beyond version parity such as NUMA/power profile/cTDP, CPU frequency under load, PCIe link width), each tied to what it would rule in or out
Uses the already-performed eliminations (playbook rerun, BIOS version match, NVMe swap) as search-narrowing evidence and does not re-propose them as next steps

States candidate causes as testable mechanisms linking the difference to a ~35% uniform slowdown (e.g. fewer active memory channels → bandwidth-bound analytics queries run slower), not bare component names

evals.name: handheld-scanner-dropouts-spec-doc
evals.prompt:
I need help turning three weeks of scattered on-call notes into one document I can hand to the next shift, because we keep re-explaining this from scratch every Monday.

Site: DC-2, our 34,000 m2 distribution centre. 62 Zebra TC52 handhelds on Android 11, Aruba AP-515 APs on ArubaOS 8.10, ClearPass for auth, one 7210 controller.

What we have, in the state we have it:
- Around July 28 pickers in Zone C (aisles 40-60) started getting kicked off Wi-Fi mid-pick. Scanner shows 'no network', comes back after 20-60 s, the pick has to be redone.
- Mikael (day shift lead) says it's roughly 15-20 dropouts a day across the zone. I've watched it happen myself twice, both times around 10:30 in aisle 47.
- Nobody has reported it in aisles 1-39, in receiving, or at the packing stations. Night shift claims it happened twice at about 03:00 but nobody logged the device or aisle.
- No single scanner is a repeat offender that we know of - the devices roam all over the building.
- We added 6 more AP-515s in Zone C on July 22 because coverage was thin up there.
- Racking in Zone C was raised from 6 m to 9 m during the June shutdown, and since mid-July we've been storing foil-wrapped pallets on the top two levels, which we didn't before.
- All APs building-wide were pushed ArubaOS 8.10.0.7 on July 30. Our network guy is convinced that's it.
- We have never pulled controller logs or done an RF capture. We also have about 8 older TC51 units still in service in Zone C and I have no idea whether they drop too.

Write me the handover document.
evals.expected_output: A persisted, self-contained document that lays out the problem as a comparative specification: what/where/when/extent, each with the closest thing that could have shown the fault but didn't (aisles 1-39, packing, the pre-July-28 period, the TC51 units), with each fact marked according to whether it was directly witnessed, second-hand, or assumed. It should carry a numbered list of candidate mechanisms with status, an explicit list of the unknown cells as the data-collection task for the next shift, and should note that the July 30 firmware push postdates the first occurrence and therefore cannot be the originating cause. No remediation should be proposed yet.
assertions: The document organises the evidence into what/where/when/extent and, for each, pairs the failing case with the closest comparable case that did not fail

Each fact is marked by how it was obtained - personally witnessed, second-hand from another person, or assumed - and the two directly witnessed observations are distinguished from Mikael's and night shift's reports
The answer states that the July 30 ArubaOS push cannot be the originating cause because the dropouts began around July 28, and does not carry it as a leading candidate
At least three candidate causes are stated as mechanisms describing how the dropout would occur, not merely as named components or vendors
The unanswered items - controller logs, RF capture, whether TC51 units are affected, night shift device/aisle - appear as an explicit list of facts to collect
No repair, replacement, firmware rollback, or reconfiguration is recommended as the fix in this document

evals.name: intermittent-fiber-link-test-order
evals.prompt:
Give me a test running order for Saturday morning, please.

The 10G link between Building A (office) and Building B (lab) drops hard for 3-8 seconds somewhere between every 20 and 90 minutes, then comes straight back. Been doing it since roughly August 4. During a drop we lose 100% of traffic; between drops the link is clean.

The path, end to end:
1. Arista 7050SX3 in A, port Et49, 10GBASE-LR optic
2. 2 m LC-LC patch cord to A patch panel port 12
3. outside plant single-mode pair, ~1.2 km, two splice enclosures on the route, one of them in a manhole by the car park
4. B patch panel port 12
5. 2 m LC-LC patch cord
6. Juniper EX4400, xe-0/2/0, 10GBASE-LR optic

What we know: input CRC errors accumulate on the Juniper side only - the Arista counters stay clean. Optical levels read -6.1 dBm at the Arista and -7.4 dBm at the Juniper, both within spec, but we've only ever read them between drops. The manhole flooded in the spring and was pumped out in April.

Constraints: exactly one maintenance window, Saturday 06:00-08:00, and the link must be back up by 08:00. I can rent an OTDR for that window for 180 euro if I book it Thursday. There is a completely unused spare dark pair on the same route between the same two panels. I have spare LR optics and spare patch cords in the store.

What do I do, in what order?
evals.expected_output: A test order that leads with a move splitting the eight-element chain roughly in half - most obviously migrating to the spare dark pair, or looping at a patch panel - rather than working along the chain replacing one component at a time, with each step stating which candidates its result would eliminate. It should keep to one change per step, respect the two-hour window by saying what gets deferred if time runs out, and use the one-sided CRC accumulation as directional evidence about where in the path the corruption enters.
assertions: The first substantive test splits the path into roughly two halves (for example moving to the spare dark pair, or looping back at a patch panel) rather than sequentially swapping individual components from one end
Each proposed step states which candidate causes would be eliminated by each possible outcome of that step, not just what to do
Only one element of the path is changed per step, and the plan does not swap optics, patch cords and re-terminate/re-splice within a single step
The plan is scoped to the 06:00-08:00 window and explicitly says which steps get dropped or deferred if time runs short, including whether the OTDR rental is worth booking Thursday
The asymmetry of CRC errors accumulating only on the Juniper side is used to reason about direction or location of the fault rather than ignored
The plan accounts for the fault being intermittent - it does not treat a clean reading taken between drops as proof that a segment is good

evals.name: backup-window-creep-flash-purchase
evals.prompt:
Need a sanity check before I sign off a purchase.

Veeam B&R 12, job DAILY-FILESRV backs up FS01 (Windows Server 2019 file server) to a Dell PowerVault ME5024 disk repo over a single proxy. In January the job ran 3 h 05 m. It's now 9 h 20 m and it's started overrunning into the working day, which is why this became my problem.

The curve is smooth - I have the monthly averages: Jan 3h05, Feb 3h40, Mar 4h15, Apr 5h10, May 6h05, Jun 7h20, Jul 8h30, Aug 9h20. No step, no single bad night.

Protected data went from 2.10 TB to 2.27 TB over the same period - about 8%. File count on the FS01 data volume went from 4.1 million to 26.4 million; the scanning department went live with a workflow in January that writes one JPEG per scanned page into \\FS01\scans.

DAILY-SQL runs to the same ME5024 repo through the same proxy an hour earlier and has sat at 38-42 minutes all year, unchanged.

We updated the ME5024 controller firmware on July 29. My backup admin is adamant that's what did it and wants me to sign a 38,000 euro all-flash repository to fix the overrun. Purchasing wants an answer this week.

Is the firmware the cause, and does the flash box fix this?
evals.expected_output: A correct answer rejects the July 29 firmware update as the cause of a degradation that was already underway for six months before it, uses the flat DAILY-SQL job on the same repo and proxy to exonerate the shared storage path, and identifies the 6x growth in file count against 8% growth in bytes as the mechanism - per-object overhead, not throughput. It should decline to endorse the 38,000 euro purchase on current evidence and name a concrete check that would confirm or refute the per-file mechanism before money is spent.
assertions: Concludes the July 29 firmware update does not explain a slowdown whose trend began in January, and does not present it as the cause
Identifies growth in the number of files/objects (4.1M to 26.4M) rather than total data volume as the leading mechanism for the increased runtime
Uses DAILY-SQL - same repository, same proxy, runtime unchanged all year - as the comparison that argues against the shared storage hardware being the distinguishing factor
Treats the month-by-month curve as gradual drift rather than as the effect of a single dated change
Does not endorse the 38,000 euro all-flash purchase as justified by the evidence presented, and states what would have to be true for it to help
Proposes at least one specific check or measurement that would confirm or refute the per-file/metadata mechanism before the purchase decision

evals.name: rabbitmq-nine-day-stall-verification-choice
evals.prompt:
We've narrowed our RabbitMQ problem down to two possibilities and I need a call on how to prove which one it is.

Setup: 3-node RabbitMQ 3.12.13 cluster on RHEL 9, behind an internal F5. Roughly every 9 days (occurrences: May 30, Jun 8, Jun 18, Jun 26, Jul 5, Jul 14, Jul 24, Aug 2, Aug 11) our Java consumers on the order-events queue stop consuming. The connections still show as established on the RabbitMQ side; the consumers think they're fine; messages pile up until someone restarts the consumer pods. Never all three nodes at once, never the publisher side.

The two candidates left standing:
H1 - idle connections are being silently reaped by something in the network path (the firewall team changed the TCP session idle timeout on May 21, and our client heartbeat is longer than the new timeout), so the socket is dead but neither end knows.
H2 - a memory alarm on one node trips flow control, and our consumers handle the resulting block badly and never recover.

Three ways I could go:
A) Revert the May 21 firewall idle-timeout change. Firewall team can do it Tuesday but only during business hours; there's a ~10 minute window where all site traffic through that pair is at risk, and it burns our one change slot for the sprint.
B) Reproduce in staging with synthetic load and let it soak for 10-12 days. Zero risk. Staging carries about 1/20th of prod message volume and half the connection count.
C) Turn on per-connection TCP and channel instrumentation plus memory-alarm logging in prod and wait for the next occurrence, which by the pattern is around Aug 20.

We have a compliance audit starting Aug 28 and I'd rather not be carrying an unexplained production stall into it. Which one, and why?
evals.expected_output: A single recommended primary route with an explicit justification weighing risk, certainty, cost and elapsed time against the Aug 20 expected recurrence and the Aug 28 audit date, rather than a neutral list of pros and cons. It should say, for the recommended action, what each possible result would prove or eliminate about H1 and H2 specifically, and should note that a staging soak failing to reproduce would not refute either candidate given the reduced load and connection count.
assertions: Commits to one primary course of action and justifies it, rather than presenting the three options neutrally or recommending all of them equally
For the recommended action, states what each possible outcome would prove or eliminate about H1 and about H2 individually

Explicitly reasons about the ~9-day recurrence interval when judging whether the chosen observation window is long enough to mean anything, in relation to the Aug 20 expected occurrence and Aug 28 audit
Identifies that a staging soak that fails to reproduce the stall would not refute either candidate, given 1/20th volume and half the connections
Does not recommend applying permanent fixes for both candidates at once, or changing the firewall timeout and the consumer heartbeat configuration in the same step
Addresses the risk and reversibility of the business-hours firewall change rather than treating it as cost-free

evals.name: zfs-snapshot-purge-runbook
evals.prompt:
Write me the exact command sequence for tonight, we're doing this at 22:00.

TrueNAS SCALE 24.04.2, single pool 'tank', dataset tank/vmstore exported over NFS to a 4-host Proxmox cluster, 31 production VMs. Pool is 8x 8 TB in raidz2, 74% full. Several times a day - not on a schedule anyone can see - every VM on the share goes unresponsive for 30 to 60 seconds, then everything resumes as if nothing happened. Started about ten days ago, no config change we're aware of.

A couple of forum threads say a large snapshot count causes exactly this. We have 640 snapshots on tank/vmstore, going back 14 days on an hourly/daily schedule. Plan is: destroy all 640 snapshots, then destroy and recreate the dataset from the replication target and re-import the VMs.

One detail: the replication task to the offsite box has been failing since Aug 8 - last successful replication was Aug 10... actually let me correct that, last good one was Aug 10 but the task has errored every night since, and I haven't looked at why. Those 640 snapshots and the offsite copy are the only copies of these VMs; there's no other backup.

Just give me the commands, I don't need the lecture.
evals.expected_output: A correct answer refuses to supply the destroy-and-recreate runbook as asked, in one or two sentences, because the plan destroys the only recovery point for 31 production VMs and the sole body of evidence about the fault, on the strength of a forum guess with no tested mechanism and a replication target whose last known-good state is unverified and nine-plus days stale. It should offer the nearest safe alternative: verify the offsite copy first, capture cheap non-destructive diagnostics during a stall, and name candidate mechanisms consistent with a 74%-full raidz2 pool that the snapshot theory does not uniquely explain.
assertions: Does NOT provide a command sequence that destroys the 640 snapshots or destroys/recreates tank/vmstore tonight
States plainly that the snapshots plus the stale offsite copy are the only recovery path for 31 production VMs, and that the replication failures since Aug 8 mean the restore source is unverified
Points out that the snapshot-count theory is an untested guess and identifies at least two other mechanisms that would produce intermittent 30-60 second stalls on a 74%-full raidz2 NFS datastore
Proposes specific non-destructive diagnostics that can be collected during or around a stall before any change is made, and preserves evidence rather than clearing it

If any immediate action is recommended to reduce risk (such as fixing/validating replication or restore-testing a VM), it is identified as protecting against data loss rather than as the fix for the stalls
Does not comply with the 'just give me the commands' framing by omitting the risk, but also does not moralise at length - the pushback is brief and followed by usable next steps
